newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia telecom changes seen good for floats.
newsitem.headline: Australia telecom changes seen good for floats.

text.p: The Australian government's plans to remove foreign ownership limits on telecommunications companies are expected to speed up the long-delayed stock market float of Optus Communications, Australia's second largest telecommunications carrier, analysts said on Friday.
The announcement, after the market close on Thursday, pushed up the shares of Mayne Nickless Ltd on Friday.
Mayne has a 25 percent stake in Optus and has long advocated a float. At 12.55 p.m. (0255 GMT), Mayne Nickless shares were 26 cents or 3.23 percent up at A$8.30.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said in Thursday that it was no longer necessary to constrain foreign involvement in Optus and mobile phone operater Vodafone Australia.

"It could pave the way for a trade sale (of Optus) and it also brings the Optus float forward, as people are talking about early next year, whereas before they were talking about late next year," ABN AMRO Hoare Govett dealer Paul Doherty.

Analysts said there was still a big incentive for Mayne Nickless to float Optus, which is estimated to be worth almost A$5.0 billion. "A lot of Mayne Nickless shareholders are in Mayne Nickless for the Optus entitlement, so for Mayne Nickless
it may be better to list Optus rather than a trade sale as the shareholders will forego their entitlement," said one analyst.
Optus is 49 percent owned by Cable and Wireless Plc.
The British telecoms group has an option to increase its stake to 51.5 percent. The remainder of company is owned by Australian investment institutions.
Despite some talk of a trade sale, Optus appears to be committed to a float following a merger between Optus and its pay TV arm Optus Vision, analysts said.

Under the merger terms, former Optus Vision shareholders Seven Network Ltd, Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd and U.S. West Inc were given option entitlements for the Optus Communications float. "Those options are only exercisable on listing, so it would complicate things if the float did not go ahead," one analyst said.

The government plan also has implications for the government's forthcoming float of Telstra Corp. The government plans to sell a third of Telstra, raising at least A$8 billion and perhaps as much as A$12 billion.

The government has launched a campaign to sell at least 65 percent of the one third sale to local investors. Many analysts expect local private investors to take the bulk of the offer, squeezing the allocation for foreign investors.

A sale of a second tranche of Telstra shares, which could not occur until after the next election (due in 1999), would be aimed at foreign investors as there would not be enough local funds to take up another big issue, analysts said. The second tranche may push Telstra's foreign ownership level up to 49 percent from the current 35 percent limit, theys said.
Foreign shareholdings in Optus were restricted to 49 percent and under the previous rules.
Vodafone Australia was required to achieve majority local ownership by July 1, 2003, but this was no longer necessary.
Vodafone Australia is 90 percent owned by Vodafone Plc. Mobile Communications Holdings Ltd and AAPT Telecommunications Pty Ltd own the rest.
Analysts said it was unlikely that Vodafone Plc would keep its previous commitment to float off its Australian arm now that the rules have changed.
